title: Keeton v. Hustler Magazine, Inc. (1984)
summary: Regular sales in New Hampshire supported a libel suit there even though the plaintiff had little personal connection to that state.
notes:
Contrast Walden, where the defendant’s challenged conduct lacked the necessary forum connection, and Bristol-Myers, where the nonresident claims were not linked to the forum conduct.

Keeton, a New York resident, sued Hustler (an Ohio corporation with its principal place of business in California) in the District of New Hampshire because its six-year libel limitations period was the only one still open; the district court dismissed, the First Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court reversed.

sections.Parties: Keeton, a New York resident, sued Hustler Magazine for libel in New Hampshire. Hustler was the defendant publisher.
sections.Material Facts: Hustler deliberately circulated approximately ten to fifteen thousand copies of its magazine in New Hampshire each month. The allegedly defamatory material was distributed there. Keeton selected the forum in circumstances involving an available limitations period, although she was not a New Hampshire resident and did not have extensive ties there.
sections.Procedural History: The jurisdictional challenge reached the Supreme Court, which sustained New Hampshire’s authority over the libel action. The assigned note emphasizes jurisdiction and the potential reach of recovery under the single-publication approach rather than providing the entire lower-court record.
sections.Issue: Could the plaintiff sue where the publisher regularly circulated the allegedly defamatory publication despite her own limited forum contacts?
sections.Holding: Yes. The publisher’s purposeful local circulation supplied the relevant connection; the plaintiff did not independently need the same kind of forum affiliation.
sections.Reasoning: The defendant had intentionally served the state’s readers. Circulation of the allegedly defamatory publication connected those commercial activities to the claim and created an interest in redressing injury associated with publication in the state. A plaintiff’s lack of residence does not eliminate otherwise sufficient contacts created by the defendant. The possibility of damages extending beyond local circulation raised additional issues, but it did not defeat personal jurisdiction. Questions about which state’s law applies remain analytically distinct.

learning.why: Regular sales in New Hampshire supported a libel suit there even though the plaintiff had little personal connection to that state.

topics.relatedness: The libel claim was connected to the magazine’s deliberate circulation in New Hampshire.
topics.purposeful-availment: Regular distribution of thousands of copies constituted exploitation of the forum market.
topics.cp-choice-law: Jurisdiction over the suit did not settle the distinct choice-of-law issues.
topics.cp-forum-shopping: Keeton chose New Hampshire solely because its six-year limitations period was the only one still open, and the Court held that motive irrelevant to jurisdiction.
topics.cp-limitations: The limitations-period differences among states drove the forum choice and the court of appeals' concern about nationwide recovery under the single-publication rule.
topics.specific-jurisdiction: The suit arose directly from Hustler's in-state circulation, so the case is a clean example of specific jurisdiction over a publisher.

mnemonic.rationale: A libel suit filed where the clock had not run
